# Accounting

What a campaign records about its own work: the dashboard, the runs' records and
transcripts its figures come from, and how cost and time are derived from them.

## 1. The dashboard

The dashboard, `crustify/artifacts/dashboard.md` unless the settings name another, is the
campaign's record of what each planner run, batch, wave and module did and cost. It is
filled from `templates/translate/dashboard.template.md`, an audit's from
`templates/audit/dashboard.template.md`, and keeps the template's format exactly.
When an adopted Crustify change adds a table or a column to the template, it is
added to the dashboard on the working branch before the next batch launches: a batch
fills the rows of the tables in place, and never adds one.

It is tracked in the campaign's tree, so every agent's worktree holds a copy, and it is
filled as the work lands rather than at the end. Each figure is measured once, where it is
produced: no suite or scan is rerun only to record one.

## 2. Cells

The dashboard's cells fall into three kinds, by when their figures can be known.

### 2.1 Landing cells

The cells measured on the tree a landing commits:

- for a batch, under the route its items' `kind` selects, as
  [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Routes section gives it: its rows
  in that route's `Batches`, tests, `Batches: safety audit` and `Batches: API stability` tables, and for a review batch in
  `Batches — review: PoC + reports`, each placed in module, wave and batch order under
  its `pass`, and for a module pass, which spans both routes, in `Module passes`; those
  tables' `Σ` rows; and the `Coverage stats` table and the Overview's LoC
  line;
- for a planner run, its row in `Planning`, but for its usage cells.

They are filled in the landing's last commit, and measured against the integration branch
tip it was rebased onto: coverage as [`testing-builds`](../../verification/testing/builds/SKILL.md)'s Coverage section measures
it, the safety audit columns as the changes in the dashboard's Safety audit metrics, and
the API stability columns as the changes to the API of the landing's items are classified. A
rebase that conflicts in the dashboard keeps every row both sides added, and the landing's
cells, `Σ` rows included, are measured again where the gates its rebase reruns cover them;
the others stand as measured on the batch's base.

An integration merge, and any merge of one branch into another, keeps every row both
sides added, and settles the rest so: an additive `Σ` cell is the sum over the merged
rows, ours plus theirs less the merge base's, and so are the Overview's `Rust LoC`
figures; a usage `Σ` cell, its per-unit cells included, sums only the rows that carry
usage, so that it is filled again with theirs; a coverage `Σ` cell, and the Overview's
`C LoC`, are the later landing's; and `Coverage stats` takes the merged suites' counts,
with the later landing's percentages until a gate measures the merged tree, which the
merge commit's message says. A table or section the template holds once is kept once,
with the rows of every copy, whether or not the merge conflicts there, and the merged
dashboard is checked for repeated headings before it is committed.

### 2.2 Usage cells

The cells known only once an agent has ended, from its usage: its cost, tokens and wall,
the per-unit costs derived from them, and their `Σ` cells. A batch's are filled on the
working branch once its row is there, once its module is integrated, as
[`versioning`](../versioning/SKILL.md) describes, or, for a port's later-stage batch, which
runs after its module's switch, once its wave is promoted. A planner run's are filled once the run is
promoted. A batch run more than once costs the sum of its runs.

### 2.3 Campaign cells

The cells that span agents: the `Module stats` table, the Overview's branch line and
test baseline, and the `Settings` lines. A module's row and the branch line are filled
when the module is integrated, and a port's module row again as each of its later-stage
waves is promoted, the baseline once it is recorded, and the `Settings` lines,
with a Notes entry, whenever a settings change is applied.

### 2.4 Side campaign cells

A side campaign keeps its own dashboard, in its own repository, and its figures are
measured there. The parent's `Side campaigns` table copies them, one row per wrapper, as
they stand at the commit the parent pins, and the `side campaigns` row of `Module stats`
sums the rows, so that the parent's `Σ campaign` covers what its side campaigns cost. A
wrapper's row is filled each time the parent's pin moves, and its `shipped at` cell when
the wrapper ships the commit the parent pins. A side campaign that serves several parents
appears in each, with the figures as of each one's pin.

An audit's dashboard follows the same kinds over its own tables.

## 3. Records

Every run's `task.json` records how its agent ran: its backend, billing, model proxy and
the arguments its CLI was given, and, once it starts, its `session_id`, which ties the run
to its session. The session's transcript, which its CLI keeps by session id, is the
agent's full log and the source of its accounting. An agent spawned as a subagent of
another session has no session of its own: its session id is `agent-<agent id>`, the
name its host gives its transcript, under the spawning session's `subagents/`.

A transcript is copied into crustify's home, as `transcripts/<session id>.jsonl`, as soon
as its agent ends, because the CLIs move and prune their own files. Its usage is derived
from the copy, as [`usage`](../usage/SKILL.md) describes, with the backend and model proxy its
`task.json` names.

An evolution review is a run like any other: its `task.json` sits in its artifact dir, and
its transcript is collected and priced the same way, its cost counted with the sessions that
orchestrate the campaign and recorded, with its tokens and wall time, in its proposal's
Review section, so that what each review bought can be weighed against its cost.

The sessions that orchestrate the campaign are collected the same way: at the start of each session, the
transcripts of the sessions before it. A resumed session keeps its id while its transcript
grows: its transcript is copied again after each run, replacing the earlier copy. The
records, transcripts and rates stay in crustify's home.

## 4. Cost and time

A run's cost and tokens are its usage's `total.cost_usd` and `total.tokens`, as
[`usage`](../usage/SKILL.md) derives them from its transcript. The computed cost is used, never a provider-reported
dollar total; under subscription billing it is the API-equivalent cost.

An agent's wall time is its usage's interval. A wave's runs from its first batch's
launch through its final review and regression gates, a review wave's in an audit through
its landing, and a module's from its first launch through its final gate.

# Versioning

How a campaign's work is held in version control: the repositories it works in, their
branches and worktrees, how a batch lands its work and how each part is promoted. Where
things sit in the tree is [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Repositories

A translation campaign produces a Rust codebase, so its repository is one: a new
repository created for the campaign, with the Rust at its root and the C it translates
inside it.

| campaign | repository | the C, under `c/` |
|---|---|---|
| wrap | `<repo>-crustify` | a submodule of the source, pinned at the campaign's revision, which the campaign never changes |
| port | `<repo>-crustify` | a submodule of the campaign's fork of the source, `<repo>-fork`, on its `main` branch, which the modules' switches trim as they leave C |

`<repo>` is the source repository's name: a campaign on libgit2 is `libgit2-crustify`,
and a port's fork `libgit2-fork`. A wrap and a port campaign share the name, since wrapping a
codebase is a step towards replacing its implementation: a port continues a wrap campaign
in its repository. Both keep the C's history where it belongs, so that it can be read in the
submodule and an upstream release taken in by rebasing the fork's `main` onto it. The fork
mirrors the source's own `main` as `upstream/main`. The repositories are created under the
`crustify-rs` organization; the campaign's tree is [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s.

A library the target uses from outside its tree is wrapped in a wrap campaign of its own,
in `<source>-crustify`, named after the source it is built from, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md) describes.

An audit reviews an existing Rust crate in its own repository, and creates none.

## 2. Branches

| branch | name | checked out |
|---|---|---|
| shipping | `main` in the campaign's own repository; `crustify/main` in an audit, beside the reviewed crate's own branches | never while the campaign runs |
| working | `crustify/devel` | in the repository's base dir |
| planner run | `crustify/planner/run-<n>` | in the repository's base dir, while its run is live |
| module | `crustify/modules/<link-unit>/<module>`, or `crustify/foundational/<link-unit>/<module>` for a foundational module | in its worktree, while it integrates |
| wave | `crustify/waves/wave-<index>` | never |
| batch | `crustify/batches/wave-<index>/batch-<index>` | in its worktree |

The shipping branch holds what the user has approved to ship: it advances only with the
user's approval, by a fast-forward to the working branch, and each advance is tagged on it,
`ship-<n>` numbered from 1, or `crustify/ship-<n>` in an audit. The working branch is where the
campaign integrates its work: planner runs fork from it and are promoted back to it, and
the modules are integrated into it, as `scheduling` describes.

A module's branch holds one run of its waves: its waves fork from
it and are promoted back to it, and it is integrated into the working branch once they
have landed, as [Integration](#45-integration) describes. `<module>` is the module's
`name`, the path of its TU or header below the C root; a path is never a directory of
another, so no two module branches collide.

A wave's branch is the integration branch its batches land on, a review wave's as much as
a translation wave's. It is never checked out: a landing push to a checked-out branch
fails, and one to a missing branch silently creates it.

An audit has no link units or modules: its waves are review waves, laid out the same
way.

Each batch has its own worktree, its `c/` a worktree of the base checkout's submodule, at

A planner run's branch is forked from the working branch's tip and checked out in the repository's base dir. Once the run has committed, the working
branch is checked out and fast-forwarded to it, and the next run forks from there.

### 5.3 Modules

A module's base is the working branch's commit that holds its scaffolded `.rs` file and
the settings it runs under, committed before its first wave.

A module's branch is forked from its base before its first wave,
once the waves of other modules that its waves depend on have been integrated. A module
whose waves the order splits, such as one that wraps a cut dependency ahead of its
consumer, or one whose wave waits for an item another module's run holds, as
[`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Wrap batches section describes, runs once per contiguous run of its waves, each run on a branch forked anew
from the working branch. In a port campaign, only the run that holds the last wave of the
module's `wrap` and `port` items switches it from C; an earlier run's integration merges
its Rust alone, the module still C. Once a run has been integrated, its branch and worktree
are purged; its end state is the working branch's commit its last run integrates into.

### 5.4 Waves

A wave's integration branch is forked from its module's branch's tip, or, for a port's
later-stage wave, which runs after its module's switch, from the working branch's tip,
before any of its batches launch, so that it exists before the first landing, as [Branches](#2-branches)
requires; that commit is the wave's base.
Once every batch has landed, the wave is promoted, as [Promotion](#43-promotion)
describes, and its branch purged.

A translation wave's review batches are batches of the wave itself, and it is promoted once
they have landed too. An audit's review waves fork as any wave does.

### 5.5 Batches

A batch's branch and worktree, forked from its wave branch's tip, are created before it
launches, with its run dir, as [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md) describes. The gitignored state its tree needs and does
not build itself, such as shared analysis databases, is symlinked from the base checkout,
and its `c/` is a worktree of the base checkout's submodule at the commit the superproject
records, since no batch changes the C.
Once the batch has landed, its worktree is purged; its branch stays until its commits are
recorded in `schedule.json`, since they are derived from it, as
[Landing](#4-landing) describes. A batch that fails keeps its branch and worktree for
inspection; they are removed before it is run again, which forks them anew.

## 6. Identity

Every commit of a campaign, in its repository and its wrappers', is authored and committed
as Crustify, whose GitHub account is `crustify-ai` and whose git identity is
`crustify <crustify@berkeley.edu>`, whatever the repository's git configuration says,
unless the settings' `identity` answer names another: an author and any co-authors, each
as `Name <email>`. The author named there then authors and commits every commit, and each
message ends with one `Co-Authored-By:` trailer per co-author and no other, none that an
agent's host suggests included.

The identity is passed explicitly, as configuration on the command line, to every command
that writes a commit, a rebase, a merge and a cherry-pick as much as a commit, since the
host may have no git identity of its own.

description: "The dashboard, its cells, the runs' records and transcripts, and how cost and time are derived. Read before filling dashboard cells or collecting a run's records."

# Accounting

What a campaign records about its own work: the dashboard, the runs' records and
transcripts its figures come from, and how cost and time are derived from them.

## 1. The dashboard

The dashboard, `crustify/artifacts/dashboard.md` unless the settings name another, is the
campaign's record of what each planner run, batch, wave and module did and cost. It is
filled from `templates/translate/dashboard.template.md`, an audit's from
`templates/audit/dashboard.template.md`, and keeps the template's format exactly.
When an adopted Crustify change adds a table or a column to the template, it is
added to the dashboard on the working branch before the next batch launches: a batch
fills the rows of the tables in place, and never adds one.

It is tracked in the campaign's tree, so every agent's worktree holds a copy, and it is
filled as the work lands rather than at the end. Each figure is measured once, where it is
produced: no suite or scan is rerun only to record one.

## 2. Cells

The dashboard's cells fall into three kinds, by when their figures can be known.

### 2.1 Landing cells

The cells measured on the tree a landing commits:

- for a batch, under the route its items' `kind` selects, as
  [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Routes section gives it: its rows
  in that route's `Batches`, tests, `Batches: safety audit` and `Batches: API stability` tables, and for a review batch in
  `Batches — review: PoC + reports`, each placed in module, wave and batch order under
  its `pass`, and for a module pass, which spans both routes, in `Module passes`; those
  tables' `Σ` rows; and the `Coverage stats` table and the Overview's LoC
  line;
- for a planner run, its row in `Planning`, but for its usage cells.

They are filled in the landing's last commit, and measured against the integration branch
tip it was rebased onto: coverage as [`testing-builds`](../../verification/testing/builds/SKILL.md)'s Coverage section measures
it, the safety audit columns as the changes in the dashboard's Safety audit metrics, and
the API stability columns as the changes to the API of the landing's items are classified. A
rebase that conflicts in the dashboard keeps every row both sides added, and the landing's
cells, `Σ` rows included, are measured again where the gates its rebase reruns cover them;
the others stand as measured on the batch's base.

An integration merge, and any merge of one branch into another, keeps every row both
sides added, and settles the rest so: an additive `Σ` cell is the sum over the merged
rows, ours plus theirs less the merge base's, and so are the Overview's `Rust LoC`
figures; a usage `Σ` cell, its per-unit cells included, sums only the rows that carry
usage, so that it is filled again with theirs; a coverage `Σ` cell, and the Overview's
`C LoC`, are the later landing's; and `Coverage stats` takes the merged suites' counts,
with the later landing's percentages until a gate measures the merged tree, which the
merge commit's message says. A table or section the template holds once is kept once,
with the rows of every copy, whether or not the merge conflicts there, and the merged
dashboard is checked for repeated headings before it is committed.

### 2.2 Usage cells

The cells known only once an agent has ended, from its usage: its cost, tokens and wall,
the per-unit costs derived from them, and their `Σ` cells. A batch's are filled on the
working branch once its row is there, once its module is integrated, as
[`versioning`](../versioning/SKILL.md) describes, or, for a port's later-stage batch, which
runs after its module's switch, once its wave is promoted. A planner run's are filled once the run is
promoted. A batch run more than once costs the sum of its runs.

### 2.3 Campaign cells

The cells that span agents: the `Module stats` table, the Overview's branch line and
test baseline, and the `Settings` lines. A module's row and the branch line are filled
when the module is integrated, and a port's module row again as each of its later-stage
waves is promoted, the baseline once it is recorded, and the `Settings` lines,
with a Notes entry, whenever a settings change is applied.

### 2.4 Side campaign cells

A side campaign keeps its own dashboard, in its own repository, and its figures are
measured there. The parent's `Side campaigns` table copies them, one row per wrapper, as
they stand at the commit the parent pins, and the `side campaigns` row of `Module stats`
sums the rows, so that the parent's `Σ campaign` covers what its side campaigns cost. A
wrapper's row is filled each time the parent's pin moves, and its `shipped at` cell when
the wrapper ships the commit the parent pins. A side campaign that serves several parents
appears in each, with the figures as of each one's pin.

An audit's dashboard follows the same kinds over its own tables.

## 3. Records

Every run's `task.json` records how its agent ran: its backend, billing, model proxy and
the arguments its CLI was given, and, once it starts, its `session_id`, which ties the run
to its session. The session's transcript, which its CLI keeps by session id, is the
agent's full log and the source of its accounting. An agent spawned as a subagent of
another session has no session of its own: its session id is `agent-<agent id>`, the
name its host gives its transcript, under the spawning session's `subagents/`.

A transcript is copied into crustify's home, as `transcripts/<session id>.jsonl`, as soon
as its agent ends, because the CLIs move and prune their own files. Its usage is derived
from the copy, as [`usage`](../usage/SKILL.md) describes, with the backend and model proxy its
`task.json` names.

An evolution review is a run like any other: its `task.json` sits in its artifact dir, and
its transcript is collected and priced the same way, its cost counted with the sessions that
orchestrate the campaign and recorded, with its tokens and wall time, in its proposal's
Review section, so that what each review bought can be weighed against its cost.

The sessions that orchestrate the campaign are collected the same way: at the start of each session, the
transcripts of the sessions before it. A resumed session keeps its id while its transcript
grows: its transcript is copied again after each run, replacing the earlier copy. The
records, transcripts and rates stay in crustify's home.

## 4. Cost and time

A run's cost and tokens are its usage's `total.cost_usd` and `total.tokens`, as
[`usage`](../usage/SKILL.md) derives them from its transcript. The computed cost is used, never a provider-reported
dollar total; under subscription billing it is the API-equivalent cost.

An agent's wall time is its usage's interval. A wave's runs from its first batch's
launch through its final review and regression gates, a review wave's in an audit through
its landing, and a module's from its first launch through its final gate.

# Porting types

How a scheduled C type is reimplemented in safe Rust: the type route, which follows
[`porting`](../SKILL.md)'s FFI boundary section and starts from
[`binding-types`](../../binding/types/SKILL.md)'s; the symbols it reaches are
[`porting-symbols`](../symbols/SKILL.md)'s.

A ported type's surface covers every field the targeted symbols touch and every lifecycle
primitive, not only those the public API publishes.

## 1. Structs

Ported storage becomes Rust-owned only once no C path accesses, allocates or frees it.
While C still owns either operation, compatible storage is retained and the blocker
reported.

A layout is ported only once no unported C of the target touches it: no field toucher,
and no other layout user. Tests and the C consumers outside the target do not count, as
[`porting-workflow`](../../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Principles section
describes, so neither a test's field access nor a definition in an installed header keeps
the layout in C. A struct whose layout another module's C still uses is wrapped where the
order places it instead, keeping its C layout behind a binding, and takes its native layout
from its `port/layout`, as [`scheduling`](../../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later
stages section schedules it.

---
name: toolchain
description: "Toolchains, edition, manifests, lints, formatting and unsafe-code rules of the generated workspace. Read before scaffolding the workspace or when a lint, format or toolchain question comes up."
---

# Rust

How the Rust a campaign generates is built, linted and formatted: its toolchains, its
edition, the lints every crate inherits and how it is formatted. What the code is named and
where it sits is [`conventions`](../conventions/SKILL.md)'s; these are the rules the toolchain
enforces on it.

## 1. Toolchains

The workspace builds and tests on stable Rust, pinned in `rust-toolchain.toml` to the
stable release current when the repository is created, with the `clippy` and `rustfmt`
components. Miri, the sanitizer and coverage instrumentation of the Rust,
BorrowSanitizer's `bsan` toolchain aside, and the formatter's unstable options need
nightly: a nightly pinned by date, recorded in the workspace manifest as
`[workspace.metadata.crustify] nightly = "nightly-<date>"`, and named explicitly wherever it
runs. A toolchain is moved forward only between waves, in a
commit of its own.

## 2. Edition and manifests

Every crate uses Rust edition 2024, with the workspace's `rust-version` set to the pinned
stable release. The shared package fields (`edition`, `rust-version`, `license`,
`repository`) are declared once, in `[workspace.package]`, and inherited. Every crate
inherits the workspace's lints with `[lints] workspace = true`.

## 3. Lints

The workspace declares its lints in `[workspace.lints.rust]` and `[workspace.lints.clippy]`.
Every gate runs with warnings denied, so a lint at `warn` fails a landing as surely as one
at `deny`; `deny` marks the lints no item may opt out of.

### 3.1 rustc

| lint | level | why |
|---|---|---|
| `nonstandard_style` (`non_snake_case`, `non_camel_case_types`, `non_upper_case_globals`) | `deny` | the naming the conventions' Naming section gives: `snake_case` functions, methods, modules and variables, `UpperCamelCase` types and traits, `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` constants and statics |
| `unsafe_code` | `warn` | unsafe code only in a module's unsafe regions, which take it back, as [Unsafe code](#5-unsafe-code) describes |
| `unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn` | `deny` | each unsafe operation in an `unsafe fn` sits in its own justified `unsafe` block |
| `missing_docs` | `warn` | every public item carries its anchor, which is a doc comment |
| `rust_2018_idioms` | `warn` | elided lifetimes in paths and other pre-2018 idioms |
| `unreachable_pub`, `unused_qualifications`, `unused_lifetimes`, `let_underscore_drop`, `trivial_casts`, `trivial_numeric_casts` | `warn` | visibility the crate does not need, and casts and drops that hide intent at the foreign boundary |

### 3.2 Clippy

| lints | level | why |
|---|---|---|
| `clippy::correctness` | `deny` | code that is outright wrong |
| `clippy::all` (`suspicious`, `style`, `complexity`, `perf`), `clippy::pedantic`, `clippy::cargo` | `warn` | as much of Clippy's stable guidance as applies; `nursery` is left out, its lints still being unsettled |
| `undocumented_unsafe_blocks`, `multiple_unsafe_ops_per_block`, `missing_safety_doc`, `unnecessary_safety_comment`, `unnecessary_safety_doc` | `deny` | every `unsafe` block is one justified operation, and every safety comment and `# Safety` section is where it belongs |
| `mem_forget`, `allow_attributes`, `allow_attributes_without_reason` | `deny` | no leak by `mem::forget`, and every exception an `#[expect]` with a reason |
| `module_inception` | `allow` | a C directory often holds a TU of its own name, so the mirrored tree nests a module in one of its name |
| `module_name_repetitions` | `allow` | items keep their C-derived names where their module, mirrored from the C path, repeats them |
| `multiple_crate_versions` | `allow` | the dependency graph is not the campaign's to dedupe |

An item that needs an exception takes it locally, as
`#[expect(<lint>, reason = "<why>")]`, never as a crate-wide `allow`: the expectation fails
once the exception is no longer needed.

### 3.3 Generated code

The raw bindings' bindgen output follows C's names and shapes, so it is exempt from the
workspace's lints: `src/sys.rs` allows every lint and lint group the workspace sets over
each generated module, under one `#[expect(clippy::allow_attributes, reason = "…")]`
naming the generated code, and the formatter skips the generated modules. The
hand-written parts of the raw bindings, such as `build.rs`, `src/sys.rs` itself and the
macro shims, follow the rest of this spec.

## 4. Formatting

Every crate is formatted by `rustfmt`, configured once in the workspace's `rustfmt.toml`:

| option | value |
|---|---|
| `edition`, `style_edition` | `"2024"` |
| `max_width`, `comment_width` | `100` |
| `newline_style` | `"Unix"` |
| `use_field_init_shorthand`, `use_try_shorthand` | `true` |
| `imports_granularity` | `"Module"` |
| `group_imports` | `"StdExternalCrate"` |
| `wrap_comments`, `normalize_comments`, `normalize_doc_attributes` | `true` |
| `format_code_in_doc_comments`, `format_macro_matchers` | `true` |
| `hex_literal_case` | `"Upper"` |
| `reorder_impl_items` | `true` |

The options from `imports_granularity` down are unstable, so the formatter runs on the
pinned nightly. A landing's tree is formatted, and the gate checks that it is.

## 5. Unsafe code

Every unsafe block carries a specific, falsifiable `// SAFETY:` comment: the invariant the
operation relies on, and why it holds on every path that reaches it. Native Rust APIs are
safe unless their caller obligation cannot be expressed in the type system; an `unsafe fn`
documents that obligation in its `# Safety` section.

Unsafe code sits only in a module's unsafe regions and in the raw bindings, as the
[conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)' Unsafe regions section describes. A region that
holds unsafe code of its own takes `unsafe_code` back where it is declared, as
`#[expect(unsafe_code, reason = "<what it reaches>")] mod ffi_import { … }`, so that the
expectation fails once the region holds none; and so does each test suite and unit-test
module that holds unsafe code. A region whose only unsafe code a macro of another crate
expands takes none: the lint does not see that code, and the expectation would fail. A
module with no region carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`, which no item within it can take
back.

name: bindgen
description: "How the raw bindings are laid out, generated, built in each mode, landed and published. Read before changing allowlists, shims, wrapper headers or build.rs, or scaffolding the bindings."
---

# Raw bindings

How a campaign's raw bindings are laid out, generated, built and shipped. They are
generated by bindgen from the C under `c/`, one module per link unit, and ship inside the
safe crate as its public `sys` module, with the C they bind: the published crate carries
the generated bindings, so that a dependent builds without bindgen or libclang, and the C
that remains, so that a dependent has the whole library and reaches what is not
translated yet through the raw bindings. How the safe crate uses them is
[`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md)'s; their lints and formatting are
[`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s Generated code section's.

## 1. Layout

```text
<repository>/
├── Cargo.toml            the safe crate's manifest; bindgen an optional build dependency
├── build.rs              builds or locates the C, compiles the C wrappers, regenerates on request
├── c/                    the C that remains, built into the crate
├── sys/<link-unit>/      one link unit's bindings
│   ├── wrapper.h         the headers they cover: the installed headers, and the internal headers its batches bind items of
│   ├── allowlist.txt     one `function|type|var <regex>` per line, filled by the batches
│   ├── external.txt      the types other link units' bindings own, one regex per line
│   ├── shims.h
│   ├── shims.c           the `crustify_<NAME>` macro shims
│   ├── bindings.rs       generated, committed
│   └── static_fns.c      generated wrappers of the allowlisted `static inline` functions, committed
└── src/sys.rs            the `sys` module: one public module per link unit, including its committed or regenerated bindings, or their doctest copy, and the re-exports of the types other link units own
```

Everything a build reads sits inside the crate, so that the packaged crate builds on its
own: no path leaves it, and `crustify/` is read only in campaign mode.

Within a link unit's Rust, `crate::sys::<link_unit>` is imported as `sys`, so that a raw
binding is `sys::<name>`, as the [conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)' Naming section spells it.
The `sys` module is public: a consumer reaches the C that is not translated yet through
it, under its C names. It takes the place of the ecosystem's `-sys` crates, and is named after them.

`c/` is the C that remains: in a wrap campaign the whole source, and in a port campaign
the fork's `main`, which each switch trims of the module it ports, as
[`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes. A build of
the crate therefore never holds both a module's C and the Rust that replaces it: the
remaining C reaches a ported module through the safe crate's exports, under their bare C
names, as the conventions' Exports section describes.

## 2. Generation

The bindings follow from the headers at the `c/` revision, the allowlists, the generator
settings below, the bindgen version, pinned exactly in `Cargo.toml`, and the LLVM pinned
below, so that generating
twice from the same input gives the same bytes. The settings are the same for every
campaign:

# Rust

How the Rust a campaign generates is built, linted and formatted: its toolchains, its
edition, the lints every crate inherits and how it is formatted. What the code is named and
where it sits is [`conventions`](../conventions/SKILL.md)'s; these are the rules the toolchain
enforces on it.

## 1. Toolchains

The workspace builds and tests on stable Rust, pinned in `rust-toolchain.toml` to the
stable release current when the repository is created, with the `clippy` and `rustfmt`
components. Miri, the sanitizer and coverage instrumentation of the Rust,
BorrowSanitizer's `bsan` toolchain aside, and the formatter's unstable options need
nightly: a nightly pinned by date, recorded in the workspace manifest as
`[workspace.metadata.crustify] nightly = "nightly-<date>"`, and named explicitly wherever it
runs. A toolchain is moved forward only between waves, in a
commit of its own.

## 2. Edition and manifests

Every crate uses Rust edition 2024, with the workspace's `rust-version` set to the pinned
stable release. The shared package fields (`edition`, `rust-version`, `license`,
`repository`) are declared once, in `[workspace.package]`, and inherited. Every crate
inherits the workspace's lints with `[lints] workspace = true`.

## 3. Lints

The workspace declares its lints in `[workspace.lints.rust]` and `[workspace.lints.clippy]`.
Every gate runs with warnings denied, so a lint at `warn` fails a landing as surely as one
at `deny`; `deny` marks the lints no item may opt out of.

### 3.1 rustc

| lint | level | why |
|---|---|---|
| `nonstandard_style` (`non_snake_case`, `non_camel_case_types`, `non_upper_case_globals`) | `deny` | the naming the conventions' Naming section gives: `snake_case` functions, methods, modules and variables, `UpperCamelCase` types and traits, `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` constants and statics |
| `unsafe_code` | `warn` | unsafe code only in a module's unsafe regions, which take it back, as [Unsafe code](#5-unsafe-code) describes |
| `unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn` | `deny` | each unsafe operation in an `unsafe fn` sits in its own justified `unsafe` block |
| `missing_docs` | `warn` | every public item carries its anchor, which is a doc comment |
| `rust_2018_idioms` | `warn` | elided lifetimes in paths and other pre-2018 idioms |
| `unreachable_pub`, `unused_qualifications`, `unused_lifetimes`, `let_underscore_drop`, `trivial_casts`, `trivial_numeric_casts` | `warn` | visibility the crate does not need, and casts and drops that hide intent at the foreign boundary |

### 3.2 Clippy

| lints | level | why |
|---|---|---|
| `clippy::correctness` | `deny` | code that is outright wrong |
| `clippy::all` (`suspicious`, `style`, `complexity`, `perf`), `clippy::pedantic`, `clippy::cargo` | `warn` | as much of Clippy's stable guidance as applies; `nursery` is left out, its lints still being unsettled |
| `undocumented_unsafe_blocks`, `multiple_unsafe_ops_per_block`, `missing_safety_doc`, `unnecessary_safety_comment`, `unnecessary_safety_doc` | `deny` | every `unsafe` block is one justified operation, and every safety comment and `# Safety` section is where it belongs |
| `mem_forget`, `allow_attributes`, `allow_attributes_without_reason` | `deny` | no leak by `mem::forget`, and every exception an `#[expect]` with a reason |
| `module_inception` | `allow` | a C directory often holds a TU of its own name, so the mirrored tree nests a module in one of its name |
| `module_name_repetitions` | `allow` | items keep their C-derived names where their module, mirrored from the C path, repeats them |
| `multiple_crate_versions` | `allow` | the dependency graph is not the campaign's to dedupe |

An item that needs an exception takes it locally, as
`#[expect(<lint>, reason = "<why>")]`, never as a crate-wide `allow`: the expectation fails
once the exception is no longer needed.

### 3.3 Generated code

The raw bindings' bindgen output follows C's names and shapes, so it is exempt from the
workspace's lints: `src/sys.rs` allows every lint and lint group the workspace sets over
each generated module, under one `#[expect(clippy::allow_attributes, reason = "…")]`
naming the generated code, and the formatter skips the generated modules. The
hand-written parts of the raw bindings, such as `build.rs`, `src/sys.rs` itself and the
macro shims, follow the rest of this spec.

## 4. Formatting

Every crate is formatted by `rustfmt`, configured once in the workspace's `rustfmt.toml`:

| option | value |
|---|---|
| `edition`, `style_edition` | `"2024"` |
| `max_width`, `comment_width` | `100` |
| `newline_style` | `"Unix"` |
| `use_field_init_shorthand`, `use_try_shorthand` | `true` |
| `imports_granularity` | `"Module"` |
| `group_imports` | `"StdExternalCrate"` |
| `wrap_comments`, `normalize_comments`, `normalize_doc_attributes` | `true` |
| `format_code_in_doc_comments`, `format_macro_matchers` | `true` |
| `hex_literal_case` | `"Upper"` |
| `reorder_impl_items` | `true` |

The options from `imports_granularity` down are unstable, so the formatter runs on the
pinned nightly. A landing's tree is formatted, and the gate checks that it is.

## 5. Unsafe code

Every unsafe block carries a specific, falsifiable `// SAFETY:` comment: the invariant the
operation relies on, and why it holds on every path that reaches it. Native Rust APIs are
safe unless their caller obligation cannot be expressed in the type system; an `unsafe fn`
documents that obligation in its `# Safety` section.

Unsafe code sits only in a module's unsafe regions and in the raw bindings, as the
[conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)' Unsafe regions section describes. A region that
holds unsafe code of its own takes `unsafe_code` back where it is declared, as
`#[expect(unsafe_code, reason = "<what it reaches>")] mod ffi_import { … }`, so that the
expectation fails once the region holds none; and so does each test suite and unit-test
module that holds unsafe code. A region whose only unsafe code a macro of another crate
expands takes none: the lint does not see that code, and the expectation would fail. A
module with no region carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`, which no item within it can take
back.

once they reach a function a shared library hides: the build fails in each, naming what
the library lacks, as system mode fails for a switched module, and bundled mode, whose
build in `OUT_DIR` has both, becomes the crate's default. The `bindgen` feature then regenerates from that build's
headers, never from an install's.

A link unit the target links as an executable, such as a command-line tool, has no
library. Bundled mode compiles its translation units as the target's build system records
them, without linking the executable, archives their objects and links the archive;
campaign mode links them from the variant's static archive, which holds them, as
[`setup`](../../workflows/setup/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes; shared and system
modes, which link libraries, refuse its feature, naming the modes that serve it. An archive
member is linked only where one of its symbols is referenced, so a test that references
the translation unit defining the executable's `main`, directly or through another member
that references it, links a second `main` beside its harness's and fails to link. That
unit's other symbols are therefore ported to exports first, so that the members which
reference them stop pulling it in, and until then the units that pull it in are tested
through the variant's executable, run as a child process.

Campaign mode serves the campaign while it extends the bindings: batches add allowlist
entries and shims, and the bindings follow from them. It needs bindgen, which the safe
crate enables for its own tests through a dev-dependency on itself with the `bindgen`
feature, so that the campaign's tests and gates regenerate while dependents build from
the committed bindings. A build that does not enable the feature, such as the crate's
documentation, uses the committed bindings unchecked; the tests and gates always enable it.
The bindings it generates are compared with the committed ones: a difference fails the
build, naming the regenerated file, unless `CRUSTIFY_BINDINGS_UPDATE` is set, in which case
they are written over `bindings.rs` and `static_fns.c`. It links the C the variant built,
so that every test runs against the instrumented C it was built for. A variant that
records a `static` archive, as [`setup`](../../workflows/setup/SKILL.md)'s Builds section
describes, has it linked statically, with the libraries its shared library links, so that
the Rust reaches the internal functions the shared library does not export, and the
remaining C resolves the exports within the same link, as bundled mode's does; only the
out-of-tree libraries' installs of the same variant take an rpath. A variant that records
none has its shared libraries linked with an rpath to them, and the test binaries export
what the remaining C resolves to, as shared mode does.

No build links two copies of a module: a mode links either a module's C or the Rust that
replaces it, never both, and the Rust static library that the target's remaining C links
from a module's switch on carries no C of its own, as the porting workflow's Builds
section describes.

## 4. Extending

The bindings grow with the batches: a batch whose items need a raw binding the bindings
lack extends its own link unit's input, and nothing else:

1. its link unit's `allowlist.txt` gains only the FFI items its items need, and
   `wrapper.h` an internal header only when one of them is declared there;
2. a shim is added to `shims.h` and `shims.c` only for a macro whose expansion depends on
   the build's configuration, as `crustify_<NAME>`, as
   [`binding-symbols`](../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Macros section describes;
3. the bindings are regenerated, in campaign mode with `CRUSTIFY_BINDINGS_UPDATE` set; and
4. the safe crate is built and tested against them.

what the re-export needs, and only that: the type joins its own link unit's `external.txt`,
the owning link unit's `allowlist.txt` too while its bindings lack the type, and the link
unit's module in `src/sys.rs` re-exports it from the owner's, under its C name.

prebuilt variant; a shim compiles with the crate, as [Build modes](#3-build-modes) describes.

A batch that changes an allowlist, `external.txt`, a shim or `wrapper.h` regenerates the
bindings and commits them in the same landing, so that the committed bindings always match
their input. The gates that check it, and that the crate packages, are
[`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section's.

## 6. Publishing

The safe crate is published with its raw bindings and the C it bundles. The packaged crate
holds the layout above, `src/`, the files of `c/` that the bundled build reads and the
C's license files, and nothing else of the repository but its README and the files the
package manager adds to every package, such as its manifest's original and its lockfile.

---
name: wavefront
description: "Deterministic queries and dependency-ordered plans over the C codebase, the first resort for any question about it: entities, uses, dependencies, pointers, lifecycles, T3 cast tables. Read before querying the C codebase, before planning, decomposing or scheduling, before analysing or binding an item, when packing wrap batches, when reviewing pointer findings or lifecycles, and before changing wavefront itself."
---

# wavefront

Wavefront answers deterministic queries about a C codebase, its entities, their uses and
dependencies, their pointers and lifecycles, and generates dependency-ordered wave plans
over it.

It is the first resort for any question about the C codebase: an entity's definition,
fields or signature, its users, callers and casts, what it depends on, and the pointer
findings and lifecycle roles submitted on it are queried rather than searched for in the
source, so that each answer covers every site the traced build compiles, and every query
of one fact gets one answer. The source is read where wavefront records nothing, to read a
body, and to judge what wavefront records.

Its `README.md` and `--help` are read in full before its first command, and each section
below names the documents under its `docs/` that its stage reads, also in full. How
wavefront scopes, orders and batches, what its configuration, tables and records hold, and
what each query returns are those documents', and are not restated here. Its goals and
non-goals, `docs/goals.md`, are what a change to wavefront is judged against, as
[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes.

## Campaign state

Wavefront's repo root is the C root: it is passed `<workdir>/c`, so that every path it
reads and reports is relative to the C root, as the plan records them. Its state sits
under `crustify/wavefront/`, which the configuration names as its `state_dir`,
`../crustify/wavefront`:

- `codeql/`, the CodeQL database and its T1/T2 tables, and `.cache`, both gitignored;
- `configs/wavefront-config.json`, the campaign's configuration, which every query of the
  bindings and reviews resolves through, with `"t3_dir": "t3"`;
- `t3/`, the T3 tables, one campaign-wide pair; and
- `ownership-store.json`, the findings submitted to it through the CLI. A finding
  submitted once is queried again rather than re-derived.

The configuration's `modules` hold one record per module of `modules.json`, named
`<link-unit>/<name>`, with ` (foundational)` after a foundational module's name.

What follows is how wavefront serves each stage: each section names the skill and section
it adds to, and states only what wavefront adds there.

## Setup

### Setup › Provisioning

CodeQL and wavefront's query pack dependencies are installed, as its README describes.
`crustify/.gitignore` lists `wavefront/codeql` and `wavefront/.cache`.

### Setup › Artifact tree

`crustify/wavefront/` is scaffolded for wavefront's state.

### Setup › Baseline

Once the builds and the baseline are recorded, the CodeQL database is created from a
traced build of the `plain` configuration in a fresh scratch dir, with `c/` as its source
root, and its T1/T2 tables are extracted, through a bootstrap configuration in
`crustify/tmp/`; the campaign's own configuration is the plan's.

## Planning

Planning reads `docs/scoping.md`, `docs/graph.md`, `docs/batching.md`,
`docs/type-lifecycle.md`, `docs/artifacts/t3.md` and `docs/artifacts/schedule.md`.

### Decomposition › Runs

Each planner run brings the configuration and the T3 tables up to date with the plan: it
emits what is missing, migrates what follows an earlier wavefront schema, adds what the
scope adds and corrects what is wrong. A changed configuration or T3 row changes the graph,
so the `todo` waves whose batches it moves are re-planned, and the `depends_on` in
`modules.json` when it moves them.

### Decomposition › Dependencies

The configuration's `modules` are authored from `modules.json`: each module's files, with
the entities its `items` list select, each by the kind it is in C. Wavefront refuses an
entry that claims what its file only declares, and a unit two modules claim, so that every
entity is owned by exactly one module; the configuration is verified against the CLI.
<!-- TODO: wavefront makes a unit of every macro an installed header defines, but of an
internal header's macro only where the closure's code expands it, so an internal API macro
no C of the closure expands is planned nowhere, and it makes units of the configuration and
attribute macros the closure expands too. It has yet to make units of the macros that are
API, and only those, count enums and
macros in the modules' records, and tell a closed enum from a flags one, which the planner
judges until then, as `scheduling`'s Later stages section describes. -->

A module's dependency records are counted from a schedule of the whole closure, without
`schedule_seeds`: its module record's `depends_on` gives its in-tree records, with their
`unique_edges` and `total_edges`; its items give the `counters`, and their references
whose `scope` is `external` the out-of-tree records.

### Decomposition › Foundational modules

The foundational modules' candidates are selected from the configuration's graph, after
the T3 tables are written, so that their cast edges resolve type-erased values: the
type-erased units that no cast edge ties to a named type, and the units whose pointers
carry the `string` property, that depend on no other module's types. Each candidate's body
is read before it is admitted. Each member's lifecycle role is identified as
`docs/type-lifecycle.md` describes and submitted to the ownership store, so that the bindings of
the foundational modules find it.

### Scheduling › Order

The link units and modules are ordered from the configuration, after its T3 tables are
written, and reviewed there:

- every type-erased parameter and field with no cast, followed until it is read as a named
  type, stored, returned or lost. A hop that dispatches on a tag and reads different types
  per branch establishes none of them;
- every cast edge wavefront derives between two public types, each that is no type
  relation dropped;
- every public type in a cast relation, the pairs that are a hierarchy recorded as
  `base_derived` rows; and
- the type-minting macros, the source checked for invocations that conditional
  compilation hides from the traced build.

A row wavefront warns is stale is corrected or deleted.

### Scheduling › Waves and batches

- A planner run schedules once, its `schedule_seeds` the files
  of the modules it plans, without batch caps: the waves' batches are packed when each
  starts. The output is written to `crustify/tmp/`, never over `schedule.json`.
- A wrap campaign schedules over the API headers alone, in wavefront's API mode.
- A unit wavefront warns belongs to no module, and a module it warns claims no unit, are
  gaps in the decomposition, corrected before the schedule is used.
- Wavefront's `modules` become `schedule.json`'s, each named back to its `link_unit`,
  `module` and `foundational`, with its `layer`, its waves and its dependency records. Its
  `depends_on.external` records group its units' references whose `scope` is `external`
  by the library whose installed headers define the referenced entity, as
  `dependencies.json` names it; the external entity's own dependencies, which wavefront
  walks too, are the side campaign's to schedule.
- Wavefront numbers its waves from 0 in every run, so the `todo` waves are numbered after
  the highest index of a started wave, in wavefront's order, their `depends_on`
  renumbered. A wave's `items` are those of its wavefront batches, with their `home`, their
  `objective`, their `used_fields` as `field_users`, a macro's `type_generator_for`
  deciding its route, and their release points. An item a started wave holds, or that a
  batch has landed with that objective, is dropped, and a dependency on it is one on that
  wave.

### Scheduling › Wrap batches

The units a batch's items depend on are their `depends_on` in the planner run's schedule,
or wavefront's dependency query over them. A wrap batch's items are closed over their wrap
dependencies by that query in API mode, less what
`scheduling`'s Wrap batches section leaves out.

### Scheduling › Later stages

A port campaign's schedule, which is not in API mode, gives each item its release
points, which `schedule.json`'s items carry as wavefront records them, and which place its
later stages: `opaque_after` a `port/layout`, `memory_unmanaged_after` a `port/memory` and
`unreferenced_after` a `port/unexport`; a macro's or a typedef's places none. A stage's
wave waits for the last waves of the modules its point's `closure.modules` names, less the
item's own; with none left, the stage is not planned, unless C tests still reference the
export once the item's module has switched, as the `scheduling` skill's Later stages
section describes. The C tests, which the closure leaves out, hold
no stage back: a `port/unexport` carries over those that still reference its export, as the
`scheduling` skill's Later stages section describes. Whether a user stays C is read from
the whole list of its users, as `docs/batching.md`'s Release points section queries them.
`memory_unmanaged_after` is `null` until the ownership store holds the raw roles, so they
are established first.

## Batches

### Versioning › Lifecycle › Batches

The CodeQL database and tables under `crustify/wavefront/codeql/`, and wavefront's
`.cache`, are gitignored state every batch needs: they are symlinked into each batch's
worktree once it is forked.

## Binding and porting

Binding and porting read `docs/pointer-properties.md`, `docs/type-lifecycle.md`,
`docs/artifacts/findings.md` and `docs/artifacts/t3.md`.

### Analysis

An item's analysis queries the campaign's configuration, and its findings are submitted
to the ownership store. A type-erased parameter or field is looked up in the T3 tables before it
is bound, and the binding names the type a row gives it rather than a raw pointer. The
instances of a type generator share one generic, with per-instance aliases.

### Binding types › Surface

A type's lifecycle primitives are identified as `docs/type-lifecycle.md` describes, and
submitted to the ownership store.

### Binding symbols › Function pointers

A function pointer's record and its users are those of wavefront's function-pointer query,
named as `docs/graph.md`'s Nodes section names it, and the sites of one written inline,
and what reaches them, are as `docs/batching.md`'s Release points section describes.
<!-- TODO: no query lists an inline function pointer's sites yet: they are read from the
table that section names. -->

### Binding symbols › Lifecycle strategies

Each foundational item's lifecycle role is in the ownership store, where planning
submitted it, and is queried for every item of the batch. A role that the item's body
contradicts is corrected in the ownership store, and the correction named in the batch's commit
message.

### Porting types

A ported type's lifecycle primitives are identified as `docs/type-lifecycle.md`
describes, and submitted to the ownership store.

## Reviewing

### Reviewing › Objectives

#### Lifecycle (`lifecycle`)

Lifecycles submitted to wavefront that are incomplete: a releaser, disposer, cloner or
constructor that the findings of the batches that bound or ported items of the type
route, or items of the foundational modules, missed, checked against the lifecycle
primitives `docs/type-lifecycle.md` identifies.

#### The submitted findings

Whatever the objectives, a review checks the pointer findings an earlier run submitted for
the workset: ownership, access, nullability, cardinality and keepalive. A wrong inference
is a finding.

#### Unsafety

The plan cuts the cycles between modules and types. A raw pointer that stands in for a
dependency a later scheduled batch wraps is such a cut, not an `unsafety` finding.

### Reviewing › Reports

A finding on wavefront's findings is filed in its own `<slug>` directory, with its report
and the evidence that proves the submitted finding wrong or incomplete, under:

- `<reviews dir>/wavefront/ownership/`, for a wrong pointer-related inference; or
- `<reviews dir>/wavefront/lifecycle/`, for an incomplete lifecycle.

A defect in wavefront itself is no finding on its findings: it is a proposal, as any tool
defect is.

### Reviewing › Fixes

Under `fix`, each corrected or completed set of findings is submitted again, and a completed lifecycle gets the representations the Rust is missing.

### Reviewing › Plan corrections

A correction of wavefront's planning artifacts is filed in the reviews sub-directory of
what it amends:

- `crustify/reviews/planner/modules/` for a configuration, with the `modules.json`
  finding it follows from;
- `crustify/reviews/planner/chased-casts/` for `chased_casts.csv`: for each `add` row the
  chain followed, hop by hop with `file:line`, or the hop that breaks it; for each `drop`
  row the cast sites that derive the edge, and why they are no type relation; and
- `crustify/reviews/planner/type-generators/` for `type_generators.csv`: the macro's
  invocation sites, conditional ones included, and the shapes they mint.

A report on a T3 table also states the DAG change the edit makes.

## Evolution

A change to wavefront reads its README's Tests section, which names its opt-in CodeQL
tests: a change to a query or a fixture's C runs them, as the `evolution` skill's Changes
section asks of a tool's opt-in tests.

### Binding symbols › Lifecycle strategies

Each foundational item's lifecycle role is in the ownership store, where planning
submitted it, and is queried for every item of the batch. A role that the item's body
contradicts is corrected in the ownership store, and the correction named in the batch's commit
message.

### Porting types

A ported type's lifecycle primitives are identified as `docs/type-lifecycle.md`
describes, and submitted to the ownership store.

## Reviewing

### Reviewing › Objectives

#### Lifecycle (`lifecycle`)

Lifecycles submitted to wavefront that are incomplete: a releaser, disposer, cloner or
constructor that the findings of the batches that bound or ported items of the type
route, or items of the foundational modules, missed, checked against the lifecycle
primitives `docs/type-lifecycle.md` identifies.

#### The submitted findings

Whatever the objectives, a review checks the pointer findings an earlier run submitted for
the workset: ownership, access, nullability, cardinality and keepalive. A wrong inference
is a finding.

#### Unsafety

The plan cuts the cycles between modules and types. A raw pointer that stands in for a
dependency a later scheduled batch wraps is such a cut, not an `unsafety` finding.

### Reviewing › Reports

A finding on wavefront's findings is filed in its own `<slug>` directory, with its report
and the evidence that proves the submitted finding wrong or incomplete, under:

- `<reviews dir>/wavefront/ownership/`, for a wrong pointer-related inference; or
- `<reviews dir>/wavefront/lifecycle/`, for an incomplete lifecycle.

A defect in wavefront itself is no finding on its findings: it is a proposal, as any tool
defect is.

### Reviewing › Fixes

Under `fix`, each corrected or completed set of findings is submitted again, and a completed lifecycle gets the representations the Rust is missing.

### Reviewing › Plan corrections

A correction of wavefront's planning artifacts is filed in the reviews sub-directory of
what it amends:

- `crustify/reviews/planner/modules/` for a configuration, with the `modules.json`
  finding it follows from;
- `crustify/reviews/planner/chased-casts/` for `chased_casts.csv`: for each `add` row the
  chain followed, hop by hop with `file:line`, or the hop that breaks it; for each `drop`
  row the cast sites that derive the edge, and why they are no type relation; and
- `crustify/reviews/planner/type-generators/` for `type_generators.csv`: the macro's
  invocation sites, conditional ones included, and the shapes they mint.

A report on a T3 table also states the DAG change the edit makes.

## Evolution

A change to wavefront reads its README's Tests section, which names its opt-in CodeQL
tests: a change to a query or a fixture's C runs them, as the `evolution` skill's Changes
section asks of a tool's opt-in tests.
